solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Threat to aircraft that's coming across in style of greeting

indicators.note: the missile is said to come across, spanning the other piece, so it wraps around it

parts.note: a SAM is a surface-to-air missile
a la, from French, means in the style of

explanation.surface: An air-defence missile approaching like a polite salutation, oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: The missile is the container, signalled by 'coming across'; 'in style of' is French a la, a phrase solvers often read as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A salaam is an Eastern salutation made with a low bow and the right hand on the forehead.

clue.text: Irresponsible and secretive about a software substitute for litmus?

indicators.note: the secretive piece goes about, around, the other pieces

parts.note: sly means secretive
pH, a measure of acidity, is what litmus paper tests for
an app is a piece of software

explanation.surface: A careless, secretive chemist using an app instead of litmus paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' makes the secretive word the container; pH is what litmus paper tests, so the question mark flags the indirect hint.
explanation.definitionFit: Casual and haphazard in manner, cheerfully careless about consequences.

clue.text: Sign name to gain access to system

parts.note: a logo is a sign or emblem

explanation.surface: Instructions to enter your name to get into a computer system.
explanation.definitionFit: Signing in to a computer network with a username and password.

clue.text: Before work, walk over high pass

indicators.note: before places the walk-and-over pieces ahead of the work piece

parts.note: an alley is a walk, a narrow path
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Before starting a job, someone takes a stroll over a mountain pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high pass' is not a col but a basketball move.
explanation.definitionFit: In basketball, a lob thrown up for a teammate to catch in mid-air and dunk.

clue.text: Location for shooting singular rock opera needs backing

indicators.note: backing says the letters found are read from right to left
the run of words singular rock opera holds the letters wanted, so they are found inside it

explanation.surface: A film location manager wants a solo rock opera played backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits reversed across 'singuLAR ROCK Opera'; 'needs' points inside the phrase and 'backing' turns it round. 'Location for shooting' suggests a film set, but it is a gunfight.
explanation.definitionFit: The corral at Tombstone, Arizona, was the site of the famous 1881 gunfight involving Wyatt Earp.

clue.text: Person fooling with spray set about new carpet

parts.note: a kidder is someone who kids, fools people

indicators.note: set about says the spray piece is placed around the new piece

parts.note: a mister is a device that sprays fine water

explanation.surface: A prankster with a spray can attacks a newly laid rug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set about' puts MISTER around N. Kidderminster is a Worcestershire town famous for carpet-making.
explanation.definitionFit: A type of reversible woven carpet named after the English town where it was made.

clue.text: Girl's mini-poem?

parts.note: a girl's name read as a lyric poem with the diminutive suffix -ette, as in kitchenette, fused onto it

explanation.surface: A short verse written by a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The name looks like a poem plus the French diminutive ending -ette, sharing the E.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, as borne by the swan princess of Swan Lake.

clue.text: Article put out after race meet

indicators.note: after says the article-and-cross pieces follow the race piece

parts.note: a run is a race
a is the indefinite article
cross means annoyed, put out

explanation.surface: A news item cancelled after a race meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' means annoyed, not removed.
explanation.definitionFit: To encounter someone by chance, to bump into them.

clue.text: Pair in cage suspended, the first to be sent down

indicators.text: the first to be sent down
indicators.note: in a down clue sending the first letter down moves it to the bottom of the word

parts.note: slung means hung, suspended

explanation.surface: A pair of birds hung in a cage, one dropped to the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of SLUNG moves from top to bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The two breathing organs sit inside the ribcage.

clue.text: Description of awfully nice gal?

indicators.note: awfully suggests the letters of the following words are badly arranged and need reshuffling

explanation.surface: How you might describe a girl who is extremely pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully' rearranges NICE GAL; the whole clue also defines, since a very nice girl might be called this.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone exceptionally sweet and good-natured is described as like a heavenly being.

clue.text: Do — but with less relish?

parts.note: do means be good enough; the condiment reading suggests cutting back on a hot yellow relish

explanation.surface: A diner's advice to eat with less of the hot sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: To succeed or be adequate, to come up to the required standard.

clue.text: When nothing legally can be done about one's dissembling, row!

definitions.text: When nothing legally can be done

indicators.note: the din goes about, surrounding, the reworked letters

parts.note: a row is a loud noise, a din

indicators.note: dissembling, disguising, hides the true order of the letters of one's

explanation.surface: A legal holiday on which a quarrel breaks out over someone's deceit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissembling' scrambles the apostrophised word and 'about' wraps the noise round it. Read 'row' as racket, not a quarrel or oarsmanship.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin legal term marks a day on which courts sit for no business, such as a Sunday.

clue.text: One laying track for a green engine

parts.note: a hen is a bird that lays eggs
RY is short for railway, a track

explanation.surface: A tracklayer working on behalf of an eco-friendly locomotive.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'green engine' is from the Thomas the Tank Engine children's stories, not an environmental motor.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Railway Series books by the Rev. W. Awdry, one of the locomotives is a green engine of this name.

clue.text: Male bears after time seen in remote areas

indicators.note: after says the male-and-bears pieces come after the time piece

parts.note: he is a male pronoun
to bear something is to stick it, tolerate it

explanation.surface: A man carrying bears, seen out in the wilderness after a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bears' is a verb meaning tolerates, not the animals.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal phrase for rural backwoods means places far from towns and civilisation.

clue.text: Penny condemned stout Glaswegian in disgrace

indicators.note: something condemned is wrecked, so the letters of stout are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: hame is the Scots word for home, and in means at home

explanation.surface: A man named Penny condemned a stout Glaswegian who was in disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'condemned' rearranges STOUT to UTTOS. HAME is Scots for home, as said in Glasgow; 'in' means at home.
explanation.definitionFit: To outshine someone so they look inferior is to embarrass or humiliate them by comparison.

clue.text: Our lot's thus working late shift

indicators.note: working suggests the letters of late shift are busy being reshaped into a new order

explanation.surface: Workers resigning themselves to doing the late shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges LATE SHIFT.
explanation.definitionFit: A resigned phrase accepting misfortune: such is our fate.

clue.text: My parking space rather confined

parts.note: coo is an exclamation of surprise, like my

explanation.surface: A complaint that a parking spot is a bit too cramped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation, not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A hutch or pen for hens is a small enclosure, cramped quarters.

clue.text: Famous Russian from history, butchered near Omsk, finally

parts.note: the past is history

indicators.note: butchered means hacked about, so the letters of near are rearranged
finally takes the last letter of Omsk

explanation.surface: A Russian figure from history, slaughtered near a Siberian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butchered' rearranges NEAR to ERNA; 'finally' takes K from Omsk.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris, the Russian poet and novelist who wrote Doctor Zhivago.

clue.text: Quietly go out on beach with recliner? Because beach is this?

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, quietly
the tide goes out when it ebbs
a lier is one who lies down, reclines

explanation.surface: Someone tiptoes away from a rocky beach with a deckchair, wondering why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go out' is the tide, not a person leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: A shingle beach is more covered in small stones than a sandy one.

clue.text: Non-standard agreement by UEFA, tho' consistently overlooked

indicators.note: letters are regularly skipped, every other one passed over, leaving the rest

explanation.surface: A slangy concession from football's European body, even if routinely ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: Skip every other letter of 'by UEFA tho'' starting with the first to leave the second, fourth, sixth and eighth.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal, slangy form of yes, expressing assent outside standard English.

clue.text: One dictated to a football team measures one's put together

parts.note: Man U is short for Manchester United
ens are printers' measures of width
I is one, so one's gives I'S

explanation.surface: A manager dictating to a football squad about its measurements.
explanation.walkthrough: Man U is Manchester United; an en is a printing measure half an em wide.
explanation.definitionFit: A secretary or scribe who writes down what someone else says is taking dictation.

clue.text: Low cape — button it around neck

indicators.note: around says the hush piece goes round the other letters

parts.note: sh means be quiet, button it
to low is to moo like a cow
C is the abbreviation for cape on maps

explanation.surface: A low-cut cape, with an order to fasten it at the neck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' is a cow's sound, and 'neck' means kiss and cuddle.
explanation.definitionFit: To kiss and cuddle amorously, as courting couples do.

clue.text: Legal action once, when reservoir location not finalised

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
a sump is a reservoir, as for oil in an engine

indicators.note: not finalised says the final letter is left off

parts.note: a site is a location

explanation.surface: An old lawsuit over where to put a reservoir, still undecided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not finalised' drops the last letter of SITE.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English common-law form of action to recover damages for breach of a simple contract.

clue.text: Passage one's going to read out

indicators.note: read out says it is the spoken form that matters, the words as pronounced

parts.note: I'll means I will, one is going to

explanation.surface: A reading of a passage that someone is about to give.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's going to' is I'LL, which is pronounced like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A walkway between rows of seats, as in a church or plane.

clue.text: Face that a woman usually has on a certain day in May?

parts.words: that a woman usually has on
parts.note: a bra is underwear a woman usually wears
VE Day, Victory in Europe, falls on 8 May

explanation.surface: A make-up face a woman puts on for a special day in spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' is a verb, not the front of the head. VE Day marks Victory in Europe in 1945.
explanation.definitionFit: To confront a danger or hardship boldly is to stand up to it without fear.

clue.text: Running time required by commercial

indicators.note: required by says the time piece is needed by, so comes after, the commercial piece

parts.note: an ad is a commercial
min is short for minute, a time

explanation.surface: A TV advert needs a certain running time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' is managing, not duration.
explanation.definitionFit: Running an organisation is the business of administration, management.

clue.text: Philosopher's informal apology including staple answer

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: including says the apology piece contains the staple piece

parts.note: soz is slang for sorry
a pin is a fastener, like a staple

explanation.surface: A thinker's offhand sorry, with a staple and an answer attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'including' signals the container; the informal apology is British text-speak, a shortening of sorry.
explanation.definitionFit: The 17th-century Dutch rationalist thinker who wrote the Ethics.

clue.text: 25 Award-winning picture of Spooner's head published

indicators.note: Spooner's says the opening sounds of the two words are swapped, as Rev Spooner did

parts.note: main means chief, head
a paper ran a story when it published it

explanation.surface: An Oscar-winning film credited to Spooner's boss, now in print.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1988 Barry Levinson film starring Dustin Hoffman won the Oscar for Best Picture.

clue.text: Visor, indeed, kept between feet, centrally

indicators.note: between says the agreeing-and-kept pieces sit inside the other letters
centrally picks out the middle letters of feet

parts.note: yes and indeed both affirm
had means kept, possessed

explanation.surface: A sun visor, indeed, held between someone's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centrally' wants only the middle pair of letters of 'feet', and 'between' sets the rest inside that pair; 'kept' is past tense, possessed.
explanation.definitionFit: A green-tinted peak worn on the forehead to keep glare off the eyes, as worn by old newsroom editors.

clue.text: Composer's brother, one released from prison

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, linking the definition to the wordplay

parts.note: Fra is the title of an Italian friar, brother

indicators.note: released from says one piece is let out of the other

parts.note: nick is British slang for prison
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A musician's brother has been let out of jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'released from' removes I from NICK, slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: César, the Belgian-born organist and composer of the Symphony in D minor.
